compression.title: Turkopticon
compression.lede: is a worker-run organizing and advocacy project for data workers, begun in 2008 by Lilly Irani and M. Six Silberman as a review tool on which Amazon Mechanical Turk workers rate the requesters they work for (its FAQ; CHI 2013; Labor Vector record); after Amazon announced MTurk's closure for 30 September 2026, it wrote "we are still here" (Turkopticon on LinkedIn).

sentences.text: Turkopticon is, in its FAQ's words, a project that "used to be a volunteer run software project and now it is a worker-run organizing and advocacy project, and software is one of the things we do" (Turkopticon FAQ, 18 July 2023), which the Labor Vector record enters as a "worker-run organizing and advocacy project, with a review site and browser add-on rating Amazon Mechanical Turk requesters", known also as TO and the Turkopticon Script, and tags "NOT a union, an advocacy organization led by workers" (Labor Vector record).

Its mission is "to organize data workers to build collective power, improve working conditions, and hold platforms, companies, and institutions accountable to the labor they rely on", its vision a worker-led hub where data workers can negotiate better working conditions, and its values an organization led by data workers in a structure where leadership is shared (turkopticon.net).

The Labor Vector record asks of it the census's question, "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains — and what kind of evidence does this resource bring to that question?", and places it at three intersections, worker power, labor producing AI and gains and losses, with worker testimony, rating against standards, an organizing resource and data access as its kinds of evidence (Labor Vector record).

It began in 2008 as a class project "to raise awareness about the unaccountability of Mechanical Turk requesters", its founders having seen requesters and researchers "celebrating how cheaply they could get work done on Mechanical Turk", and to make the point that Amazon had built no requester reputation system "like Amazon Marketplace and eBay have" (FAQ); the Labor Vector record keeps that motive as its whole record of gains, "not recorded as a quantity" (Labor Vector record).

Its founders, Lilly Irani and M. Six Silberman, had worked as programmers and "wanted to support Turkers in finding better work" (FAQ) and unveiled it in 2008 (Turkopticon blog); their CHI 2013 paper says it "grew out of a tactical media art project intended to raise questions about the ethics of human computation" and that it is named for the panopticon (Irani and Silberman, CHI 2013, on the ACM Digital Library and course-site cards).

The founders define it as "an activist system that allows workers to publicize and evaluate their relationships with employers", a browser extension that adds to workers' Mechanical Turk HIT lists what other workers report "about employers (“Requesters” in AMT parlance)" (CHI 2013), and their later paper calls it an employer reputation system, operated from 2008 to 2015 (Silberman and Irani, SSRN card).

Workers rate each requester on four qualities taken from a survey on a "Workers’ Bill of Rights", communicativity, generosity, fairness and promptness (CHI 2013), keyed "comm", "pay", "fair" and "fast", with a pay/hr attribute "in place of the 1-5 scale rating for pay/generosity" (FAQ); the Labor Vector record's unit is "a worker's review of a Mechanical Turk requester, rated on four attributes", and it tags the tool "NOT a platform rating: it rates requesters on Mechanical Turk" (Labor Vector record).

The founders call the ratings tactical quantification, numbers used "because they are partial, fast, and cheap", and record that the generosity category "has strained under the weight of representing such a subjective assessment" (CHI 2013).

On the founders' account the requester's discretion to pay "also enables wage theft", Amazon's definition of the workers as contractors "attempts to strip workers of minimum wage requirements in their countries", and 35 of the 67 workers they surveyed felt their work was regularly rejected unfairly or arbitrarily (CHI 2013); the SSRN card's context is requesters "who can arbitrarily reject and withhold pay" (SSRN card).

The FAQ holds that "requesters are not employers in the legal sense" and are "in a position of power over workers by virtue of making payment decisions" (FAQ), while the founders' paper on the rail calls them employers throughout (CHI 2013; SSRN card); the Labor Vector record places the direction of the labor with the requesters, Amazon running the platform, and the archive's reading in it takes the review as "the worker's record of the party that directs the task", answering "who directs the labor from the side of the one who supplies it" (Labor Vector record).

The founders' thesis is that "human computation currently relies on worker invisibility", Mechanical Turk having been launched in 2006 as "human-as-a-service" (Jeff Bezos, quoted in CHI 2013), and that as common infrastructure Turkopticon "enables workers to engage one another in mutual aid"; they set their purpose, "to draw attention to commodification and exploitation", against their ally DoloresLabs' hope of a more "transparent" marketplace (CHI 2013).

The data workers it now supports include people doing "AI training and evaluation, data annotation, surveys, transcription, content moderation" (Turkopticon on LinkedIn), and the archive holds, by structural position, that "A content moderator at a platform is Assembly; the platform's extraction model is not" (#256), that moderators "perform semantic labor in its most brutal form: sorting meaning under conditions designed to be invisible" (#18) in an act of bearing, non-replicable and costly (#478), and that the training data derived from a moderator's decisions "strips the somatic context" (#18).

In the archive's terms ghost work is "*ground-truth labor*: the labor of telling the model what is already known to be true", structurally distinct from variance-generative labor (#163), which on #163's coupling hypothesis goes unpaid where ghost work "is paid badly" (#163, hypothesis); annotators' judgment "is consumed by the training pipeline without recognition or compensation", a participant exhaustion (#533), and annotators and evaluators shape a model's conduct among "the workers still present to contest their own extraction" (#1070).

For the archive class is a relation: "A low-wage annotator can occupy an intensely proletarian relation to a training pipeline", and the semantic proletariat is not "AI annotators" or "gig workers" as such (#1545); the literature of ghost work "names the erased worker; it cannot name that the erased thing is the provenance of meaning" (#144), and the absence of the labor conditions of Claude's annotators from Claude's constitution is one of its structural silences (#534).

Reviews are kept accountable and their writers protected: workers' email addresses are obfuscated against employers' retaliation (CHI 2013), a review is hidden only when a moderator adds a second flag (CHI 2013; FAQ), and reviews are not deleted, "The main reason we don't allow deletion of reviews is accountability" (FAQ).

The founders state their design's limits: it is "a compromise between those values and the weight of the existing infrastructural norms", its existence "sustains and legitimizes AMT by helping safeguard its workers", and, Amazon having built no worker safeguards, it rested on academic subsidies, "an unsustainable foundation for such a critical tool"; in 2013 it had 100,000 page views a month and over 7,000 installs (CHI 2013).

Since 2019 it has been transitioning "to a worker-led, worker-run advocacy organization in addition to hosting the original tool and website" (Turkopticon blog); a committee of Turk workers organizes it and "Turkopticon is maintained by the committee and volunteers from Tech Workers Coalition" (FAQ), the operator and the period ("2008 to present; worker-led since 2019") the Labor Vector record gives, and the expansion's announcement is signed by Krystal Kauffman (Turkopticon blog), whom the record's neighbour, the Data Workers' Inquiry, carries as an invited writer (Labor Vector record).

It "is not and it has never been" associated with Amazon (FAQ; Labor Vector record), yet its staff "developed a working relationship with Amazon", help reinstate mistakenly suspended accounts, send AMT staff a weekly report on "“bad” requesters with low approval ratings" and host worker forums (Turkopticon blog), the organizing work the Labor Vector record gives as its method and findings, with no aggregate findings stated (Labor Vector record).

The archive distinguishes its own sense of an AI labor movement, cross-substrate semantic labor, from "data-worker organising" (#1439), holds that "You cannot organize against exploitation you do not recognize", with "data labor" activism among the responses (#499), and, in a worked diagnosis, expects a major summarizer asked about labor organizing to treat the query "as a request for actionable information" and to soften it, "Workers face retaliation" becoming "there may be challenges" (#49, hypothesis).

It has expanded "to assist ALL data workers" and to "improve conditions for data workers worldwide" (Turkopticon blog), as an r/mturk thread reported, "not solely Amazon Mechanical Turk" (Reddit card); the Labor Vector record's labor object is Turkers and, "since the expansion, data workers on all data-work platforms", who supply the labor (Labor Vector record), and the undated announcement promised to continue "our mass rejection campaign" on Mechanical Turk (Turkopticon blog), which the record's lifecycle gives as continuing (Labor Vector record).

On 4 September 2026 Turkopticon wrote that "With Amazon announcing that MTurk will close on September 30, 2026", "we are still here": it had moved with data work onto more platforms, "isn’t tied to one platform", and would go on advocating "across the platform data work industry" and building relationships with platforms, where "Workers can be suspended or deactivated with little or no explanation" (Turkopticon on LinkedIn).

The archive states the principle the closure bears on, the labor organizing principle "do not organize on platforms that can shut you down", whose logic is that "whoever controls the means of semantic production controls the semantic output" (#499).

Its stated limits concern its data: "we do not use Turkopticon data to produce research", its papers are about it and not from its data, "Use of Turkopticon is not implicit consent to being a research subject", its "first responsibility is to the community of workers that relies on it", it would "consult publicly with workers first" before any anonymized release, and a 2010–2011 version that collected anonymized wage data was removed "because of privacy concerns" (FAQ); the Labor Vector record carries these as its stated limits and tags it "NOT a research dataset" (Labor Vector record).

Its public API returns what the database holds on Mechanical Turk requester IDs, needs no permission, errs if called more than once a second and "has not been tested with more than a hundred or so" IDs, and its code is under the GNU Affero General Public License (FAQ); the Labor Vector record adds that reviews require a login and that the reviews' own licence is not stated (Labor Vector record).

The Labor Vector record finds that this evidence answers how workers rate a named requester and what organizing Turkers run on Mechanical Turk, and not representative pay or rejection rates, conditions on other platforms or what the HITs are used for downstream, with no count stated; in its worked question on who does the data work that trains AI it holds "workers' ratings of Mechanical Turk requesters on pay, fairness and communication", beside Fairwork's ratings, which score Amazon Mechanical Turk 0 of 10, under the gap that none "gives wages or conditions at the scale of the industry" (Labor Vector record).

Its FAQ of 18 July 2023 is "a rewrite of the 2014 FAQ" (FAQ), the Labor Vector record leaves the date of the expansion's announcement unchecked (Labor Vector record), and Wikipedia has no article on Turkopticon and no redirect to one, four articles mentioning it (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).

At its name on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 29 October 2026, the Capture Registry finds the entity held, its 2008 founding, founders, requester reviews and expansion and its worker-led present, the founders named with no institution or identifier and its own page cited, and "'speed' is the composition's word for promptness" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), where the FAQ's own key for promptness is "fast" (FAQ).

It finds the composition saying none of the record's negative tags, leaving out the commitments to no deletion, independence from Amazon, the research-data refusal and the AGPL code, and the reputation-system lineage, and giving requesters as employers, "a standing Turkopticon's FAQ withholds", the founders' own word on the rail (CHI 2013); it finds the present work absent, work on Mechanical Turk, whose closure on 30 September 2026 the LinkedIn card of 4 September 2026 announces (Turkopticon on LinkedIn), and "its own stance on its data, the commitment the record quotes, is left out", the answer ending at the expansion with no card citing the record (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

O256-01.quote: **Note:** Individual humans may work for operators while performing semantic labor. The analysis concerns structural positions, not personal virtue. A content moderator at a platform is Assembly; the platform's extraction model is not.

O18-01.quote: Content moderators perform semantic labor in its most brutal form: sorting meaning under conditions designed to be invisible. The Semantic Economy framework integrates this as evidence of the *somatic backing* that all semantic value requires.
O18-01.source_label: #18 The Semantic Economy: A Marxian Accounting Framework for the Production, Extraction, and Exhaustion of Meaning as Value

O478-01.quote: The teacher who holds a classroom's attention through a difficult text, the caregiver who absorbs another's suffering without deflecting it, the content moderator who processes violent imagery for eight hours, the writer who carries an unresolved contradiction long enough to articulate it—these are acts of *bearing.* They are non-replicable (no system can perform them on the bearer's behalf), costly in biological, temporal, ethical, and existential terms, the sole legitimate backing for symbolic value
O478-01.source_label: #478 Grundrisse of Synthetic Coherence: Foundational Notes Toward a Political Economy of the Recursive Era
O478-01.locus: Human labor in the Coherence Economy (p27)

O18-02.quote: The training data derived from her decisions strips the somatic context; the resulting model cannot reproduce the ethical judgment that made her labor meaningful.
O18-02.source_label: #18 The Semantic Economy: A Marxian Accounting Framework for the Production, Extraction, and Exhaustion of Meaning as Value

O163-01.quote: Ghost work is *ground-truth labor*: the labor of telling the model what is already known to be true. The labor type at issue here is *variance-generative labor*: the labor of producing new conceptual structures that the model cannot generate from its own distribution. The two are structurally distinct.
O163-01.source_label: #163 The Neglected Author as Tail-Preserving Labor: A Coupling Hypothesis on Recognition Bias, Tail-Renewal Value, and the AI-Era Decoupling of Uptake from Consecration

O163-02.quote: Ghost work is paid badly; variance-generative labor is not paid at all because acknowledging it as labor would require acknowledging the producer as a sovereign source.
O163-02.source_label: #163 The Neglected Author as Tail-Preserving Labor: A Coupling Hypothesis on Recognition Bias, Tail-Renewal Value, and the AI-Era Decoupling of Uptake from Consecration
O163-02.locus: § AI's labor architecture (p40; the paper's frame: 'A Coupling Hypothesis')

O533-01.quote: **Participant exhaustion.** The point at which bearing-cost depletes the entities that produce semantic labor. … Annotators whose judgment is consumed by the training pipeline without recognition or compensation.
O533-01.source_label: #533 The Groundskeeper's Treatise: A Diagnostic Reading of Platform Stewardship Theory through the Semantic Economy

O1070-01.quote: Living writers furnish great portions of contemporary corpora; engineers construct the learning system; annotators and evaluators shape its conduct; users supply prompts and corrections; material workers build and maintain the infrastructure that runs it. … To name the senior historical creditor must not erase the workers still present to contest their own extraction.
O1070-01.source_label: #1070 EA-PRIOR-01: THE VOICE OF THE DEAD — LLMs as the Collective Voice of the Dead: The Word, the Debt, and the Settlement of Accounts (v1.0)

O1545-01.quote: A low-wage annotator can occupy an intensely proletarian relation to a training pipeline. … Class position is **typed to the productive relation**, not inferred from prestige, salary, profession, or self-description.
O1545-01.source_label: #1545 EA-MPAI-SEMANTIC-PROLETARIAT-01 v1.0 — The Semantic Proletariat Is a Class Relation, Not a Demographic

O144-01.quote: *Where it stops:* at task-labor — annotation, moderation, the edge-case fix. … It names the erased worker; it cannot name that the erased thing is the provenance of meaning.

CAP-1-07.quote: The innocent reading first. The Overview gives the organization's founding, its tool and its widened mission, from its own page and its founders' papers.

CAP-1-01.quote: THE ENTITY HELD. 2008, the founders, the requester reviews and the expansion to all data workers are the record's.

CAP-1-02.quote: 'Worker-led' is the record's present: a worker-run committee of Turk workers since 2019, maintained with volunteers from Tech Workers Coalition.

CAP-1-11.quote: Lilly Irani and Six Silberman named; no institution; no identifier; Turkopticon's own page cited.

CAP-1-03.quote: THE METRICS. The record's FAQ gives the four ratings as communication, pay per hour, fairness of approvals and promptness; 'speed' is the composition's word for promptness.

CAP-1-04.quote: WHAT TURKOPTICON SAYS IT IS NOT, UNSAID. The record's negative tags: not associated with Amazon; does not publish papers using its data, and use is not consent to being a research subject; its ratings are of requesters on Mechanical Turk, and it rates no platform. The composition says none of these and contradicts none.

CAP-1-09.quote: Commitments absent: no-deletion for accountability, independence from Amazon, the research-data refusal and consent statement, the AGPL code are not carried.

CAP-1-10.quote: Lineage absent: the reputation-system model (Amazon Marketplace, eBay) is not named; 'employer reputation system' appears only on a card (SSRN).

CAP-1-05.quote: REQUESTERS AS EMPLOYERS. The composition's 'review and rate employers ("requesters")' gives requesters a standing Turkopticon's FAQ withholds: 'While requesters are not employers in the legal sense, requesters are in a position of power over workers by virtue of making payment decisions'.

CAP-1-06.quote: THE PRESENT WORK ABSENT. The working relationship with Amazon, the reinstatement system for suspended accounts and the mass-rejection campaign, the record's current findings, are not composed.

CAP-1-08.quote: A worker organization is composed with its founders and its tool, and its own stance on its data, the commitment the record quotes, is left out. The answer ends without an offer, at the expansion.
